text_blocks.snippet: The early signs of type 2 diabetes often develop slowly over several years, and some people experience no symptoms at all.
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the Mayo Clinic, common early warning signs include:

snippet_links.text: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

list.snippet: Increased thirst and frequent urination: High blood sugar forces your kidneys to work overtime to filter and absorb excess glucose. When they cannot keep up, excess sugar is excreted into your urine, pulling fluids from your tissues and causing dehydration.
Constant fatigue: If glucose cannot enter your cells properly, your body lacks its primary source of energy, leaving you feeling exhausted even after resting.
Increased hunger: Because your cells are not getting the glucose they need for fuel, your body may signal a constant need for more food shortly after eating.
Blurred vision: Fluctuating fluid levels can cause the lenses in your eyes to swell, changing their shape and making it difficult to focus.
Slow-healing cuts or sores: Elevated blood sugar impairs your immune response and blood circulation, making minor scrapes, cuts, or infections take much longer to heal.
Tingling or numbness: Mild peripheral nerve damage can cause a prickling sensation or numbness, typically starting in the hands or feet.
Darkened skin patches: A condition called acanthosis nigricans causes dark, velvety patches of skin to form in body folds, such as the neck, armpits, or groin, which can signal insulin resistance.
Frequent infections: Higher sugar levels in bodily fluids create an environment where bacteria and yeast thrive, leading to recurring urinary tract or yeast infections.

text_blocks.snippet: If you suspect you may have type 2 diabetes, sharing your current symptoms or whether you have risk factors like family history or age over 45 can help me provide more tailored guidance on when to see a doctor for blood testing.
